propositions.text: The Principal Appellant is a Haitian citizen and his minor daughters are US citizens; he represents them.
propositions.quote: The Appellants, XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) is a citizen of Haiti, and his minor daughters XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are citizens of the United States of America (U.S.). The Principal Appellant is the designated representative of the minor Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant is a Haitian citizen and his minor daughters are US citizens; he represents them, says the court.

propositions.text: The RPD found the spouse/mother established nexus to a social group and risk of gender-based persecution.
propositions.quote: The claim of the Appellants' spouse/mother was joined to those of the Appellants, and the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that she established a nexus to membership in a particular social group and that she would face more than a mere possibility of gender-based persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the spouse/mother established nexus to a social group and risk of gender-based persecution, reports the court.

propositions.text: The RPD found the Principal Appellant did not establish nexus to a Convention ground and had credibility issues.
propositions.quote: The RPD found the Principal Appellant did not establish a nexus to a Convention ground, identified credibility issues and concluded that the Principal Appellant did not provide sufficient credible evidence that he is personally at risk in Haiti.

propositions.text: The RPD found the minor Appellants made no allegations against the US.
propositions.quote: The RPD also found that the minor Appellants did not make any allegations against the U.S.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Principal Appellant lacked nexus and credibility; minor Appellants made no US allegations, says the court.

propositions.text: The Appellants identify issues with the RPD decision and submit new evidence under IRPA section 110(4).
propositions.quote: The Appellants identify several issues with the RPD decision. The Appellants submit new evidence under section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and seek a hearing pursuant to section 110(6).

propositions.text: Some new evidence is accepted but the request for a hearing is denied.
propositions.quote: I have accepted some of the new evidence but deny their request for a hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants submit new evidence and seek a hearing; the court accepts some evidence but denies the hearing request.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant did not establish prospective risk in Haiti or risk to minors in the US.
propositions.quote: Following my own review, I find that the Principal Appellant did not establish that he faces a prospective risk in Haiti or that the minor Appellants face a serious possibility of persecution or risk in the US.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Principal Appellant did not establish prospective risk in Haiti or to minors in the US.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed; the RPD was correct that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: Some evidence presented by the Appellants is accepted as new evidence.
propositions.quote: NEW EVIDENCE Some the evidence presented by the Appellants is accepted

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, agrees with the RPD, and accepts some new evidence from the Appellants.

propositions.text: The claims were heard on Feb 17, 2020; RPD decision on Feb 24, 2020; new evidence presented Sept 25, 2020.
propositions.quote: The Appellants' claims were heard on February 17, 2020, and the RPD gave its decision on February 24, 2020. The Appellants presented new evidence with the perfection of their appeal on September 25, 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The claims were heard in February 2020; new evidence was presented in September 2020, says the court.

propositions.text: Section 110(4) of IRPA allows new evidence only if it arose after rejection or was not reasonably available then.
propositions.quote: Section 110(4) of the IRPA provides that an appellant may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

propositions.text: Singh requires a narrow interpretation of section 110(4) with no RAD discretion; new evidence must meet credibility, relevance, newness.
propositions.quote: In Singh,1 the Federal Court of Appeal dictates a narrow interpretation of section 110(4): the conditions set out therein must be met, and there is no room for discretion on the part of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) . If the section 110(4) threshold is met, then the new evidence must also meet jurisprudential requirements of credibility, relevance and newness.2

paragraphs.summary: Section 110(4) of IRPA and Singh require narrow new evidence criteria and no RAD discretion, explains the court.

propositions.text: The Appellants presented ten pieces of new evidence including letters and reports from credible sources.
propositions.quote: The Appellants presented the following new evidence with the perfection of their appeal: A. Letter dated "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX" from the Principal Appellant's friend, XXXX XXXX XXXX;3 B. Letter undated from the Principal Appellant's friend, XXXX XXXX XXXX;4 C. Letter dated Tuesday, XXXX XXXX XXXX 2020, from the Principal Appellant's friend, XXXX XXXX;5 D. Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada, Haiti: Treatment by society of Haitians who have lived for a long time abroad, especially in Canada, after they return to their country; whether they are at risk of being victims of violence, and including the type of violence and from whom; whether their return could represent a threat to their families (2018-August 2020), HTI200334.FE, 27 August 2020;6 E. JosÚ Miguel Vivanco, Concerns Raised Over Planned Gang Raid in Haiti, Human Rights Watch, April 28, 2020;7 F. Unattributed, The bandits control the territory": resurgence of armed violence in Haiti, France Media Agency, August 5, 2020;8 G. Jacqueline Charles, Criminal gangs for hire: Corrupt cops and the fight for votes in Haiti's next elections, Miami Herald, June 26, 2020;9 H. Unattributed, Haiti - Insecurity : 616 victims of homicides in 5 months, Haiti Libre, June 23, 2020;10 I. Haiti 2020 Crime & Safety Report, Overseas Security Advisory Council, Bureau of Diplomatic Security, U.S. Department of State, April 29, 2020;11 J. Unattributed, US Urges Citizens to Stay Away From Haiti, PRIDE, March 6, 2020.12

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants presented ten new evidence items including letters and reports, says the court.

propositions.text: RAD Rules require appellant's memorandum to detail how new evidence meets section 110(4) requirements.
propositions.quote: The RAD Rules are very clear that the appellant's memorandum must include full and detailed submissions regarding how any new evidence meets the requirements of section 110(4).13

propositions.text: The Appellants did not make submissions about how the new evidence meets section 110(4).
propositions.quote: The Appellants did not make any submissions about the new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD Rules require detailed submissions on new evidence; the Appellants made none, says the court.

propositions.text: Documents A, B, C are undated or unsigned letters lacking credibility and are inadmissible as new evidence.
propositions.quote: Documents A, B and C are typewritten letters from friends of the Principal Appellant. Document A does not specify the year in the date, document B is not dated at all and none of documents A, B or C are signed. There is no indication how these letters were received by the Appellants and no documents to confirm the identity of the authors are provided. I do not find that documents A, B and C are credible on their face and, therefore, are not admissible as new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds letters A, B, C lack credibility and are inadmissible as new evidence.

propositions.text: Documents D-J meet temporal threshold and are admissible as new evidence; some are in the National Documentation Package.
propositions.quote: Documents D-J were produced after the RPD decision, so they meet the temporal threshold of section 110(4). Documents D14 and I15 are found in the current version of the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Haiti. Documents E, F, G, H and J are new, published by credible news sources and are relevant to the appeal as an update to country conditions. I find that documents D-J are admissible as new evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Documents D-J meet timing and credibility requirements and are admissible as new evidence, finds the court.

propositions.text: The Appellants request an oral hearing before the RAD.
propositions.quote: The Appellants request that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) hold a hearing.

propositions.text: Section 110(6) of IRPA allows a hearing only if new evidence raises serious credibility issues, is central, and could change the claim outcome.
propositions.quote: Section 110(6) of the IRPA says the RAD may only hold a hearing if there is new evidence that (a) raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, (b) is central to the RPD's decision, and (c) if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

propositions.text: The new evidence relates to country conditions and does not raise credibility issues; hearing request is denied.
propositions.quote: Since the new evidence I accepted relates to country conditions and does not raise an issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, it does not meet the 110(6) criteria. The hearing request is denied.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants request a hearing; the court denies it as new evidence does not raise credibility issues, citing IRPA section 110(6).

propositions.text: The RAD reviews RPD decisions on correctness standard, except for deference on oral testimony assessment.
propositions.quote: The RAD reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing and weighing the oral testimony heard, which in particular cases attracts deference.16 Unless specifically stated below, I have applied the correctness standard.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reviews RPD decisions on correctness standard, except deference for oral testimony assessment, says the court.

propositions.text: Whether the RPD was correct in finding the Principal Appellant did not provide sufficient credible evidence of personal risk in Haiti.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue is whether the RPD was correct in finding that the Principal Appellant did not provide sufficient credible evidence that he is personally at risk if he returns to Haiti.

paragraphs.summary: The key issue is whether the RPD was correct that the Principal Appellant lacked credible evidence of personal risk in Haiti.

propositions.text: The Appellants argue the RPD erred by making a perverse decision, failing to analyze corroborating evidence, and failing to assess forward-looking risk.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in: making its decision in a perverse or capricious manner without regard to the evidence presented; failing to analyze evidence which corroborated the personal risk of the Principal Appellant as a wealthy returnee; and failing to assess and consider the evidence and provide a forward-looking assessment of risk.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants argue the RPD erred by ignoring evidence and failing to assess forward-looking risk, says the court.

propositions.text: The Appellants make no arguments about minor Appellants' risk in the US; the court sees no reason to disturb RPD's finding.
propositions.quote: The Appellants do not make any arguments about the RPD finding that the minor Appellants do not face a serious possibility of persecution or risk in the U.S. and I see no reason to disturb the RPD finding.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no reason to disturb the RPD's finding on minor Appellants' risk in the US, as no arguments were made.

propositions.text: The RPD did not fully analyze the Principal Appellant's prospective risk; the court has done so and finds no risk on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: Following my review of the record, the testimony, the Appellants' arguments and new evidence, I agree that the RPD did not undertake a fulsome analysis of the Principal Appellant's prospective risk, so I have done so. I find that the Appellants did not establish, on a balance of probabilities, that they face a prospective risk to their lives or to cruel and unusual punishment in Haiti.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD failed full analysis; after review, the court finds no prospective risk to the Appellants in Haiti.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant testified about fear of an unknown gang attacking his home in 2018.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant originally testified that he was afraid of "the gang" who attacked his home on XXXX XXXX, 2018, who were "not people that [he] knew."17

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant initially did not know why he was attacked but later said it was because they believed he was rich.
propositions.quote: When the RPD asked why he thought he was attacked, the Principal Appellant answered, "Well, I don't know the reason."18 When his counsel asked him later in the hearing, the Principal Appellant said that "because for some reason they believe that I am rich."19

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant testified about a 2018 gang attack and later said it was due to perceived wealth, reports the RPD.

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant testified about multiple incidents in 2018-2019 including threats, attacks, robbery, and family harm.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant testified that his problems in Haiti started in XXXX 2018 and he presented the evidence about the following incidents: Date Target Event BOC Testimony Other XXXX and XXXX 2018 Principal Appellant Anonymous telephone death threats to Principal Appellant "I received some messages and anonymous phone calls from my work wanting me to do corruption"20 Certificat de plainte, Le XXXX XXXX 201821 XXXX XXXX, 2018 Principal Appellant and spouse Attack by unidentified armed and masked individuals who fired on their car "XXXX 2018, we were mistreated by a mask person...he fired two gun shot on my vehicle"22 Spouse's statement23 Certificat de plainte Le XXXX XXXX 201824 XXXX XXXX, 2018 Appellants' residence Intrusion, damage and robbery by armed unidentified individuals XXXX 2018 house was attacked by gang of armed people, broke the gate and the front of the house, stole a lot of stuff and killed dogs25 "...on XXXX XXXX, 2018 ...gangsters entered my house and they were shooting and they said that they would rape and kill my family"26 Spouse's statement27 Certificat de plainte Le XXXX XXXX 201828 XXXX XXXX, 2018 Principal Appellant's father-in-law's bag Two armed and unidentified bandits stole bag DÚclaration de perte29 XXXX XXXX, 2019 Principal Appellant's father-in-law's business Fire which started at a neighbour's burnt construction materials Extrait des minutes du Greffe30 XXXX XXXX, 2019 Principal Appellant's mother Victim of physical aggression ...when they attacked my mom they said if they found me they would kill me because I left and they are still looking for me.31 ProcÞs-verbal du XXXX XXXX 201932 Certificat mÚdical33

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Appellant testified about multiple 2018-2019 incidents including threats, attacks, robbery, and family harm, reports the RPD.

propositions.text: All Appellants and spouse/mother travelled to Canada after attack on their home in 2018.
propositions.quote: all the Appellants and their spouse/mother travelled to Canada the day after the attack on their home

propositions.text: Principal Appellant returned to Haiti and came back to Canada in 2018.
propositions.quote: he returned to Haiti and came back to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2018

propositions.text: Principal Appellant did not make asylum claim in Canada immediately due to pressure and uncertainty.
propositions.quote: No, I didn't do that yet because I was somewhat under pressure so much. I was not sure exactly what am I going to do next.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant travelled extensively before leaving Haiti, including five visits to the U.S.
propositions.quote: He said that he visited the U.S. five times.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says all travelled to Canada after 2018 attack; Principal Appellant returned to Haiti then Canada; delayed asylum claim; travelled widely before leaving Haiti.

propositions.text: RPD found no nexus to Convention ground; claim fails under section 96 due to targeting by criminals for perceived wealth.
propositions.quote: he did not establish a nexus to a Convention ground and his claim fails under section 96

propositions.text: Appellants do not challenge RPD's finding on nexus and claim failure.
propositions.quote: The Appellants do not make submissions about this finding

propositions.text: I find RPD did not err in this finding.
propositions.quote: I find that the RPD did not err.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found no nexus to Convention ground; applicant does not challenge; court agrees RPD did not err.

propositions.text: RPD found Principal Appellant's failure to claim asylum and re-availment to Haiti undermined credibility and risk evidence.
propositions.quote: failure to make an asylum claim in Canada and re-availment to Haiti undermines his credibility

propositions.text: RPD found insufficient credible evidence of personal risk if returned to Haiti.
propositions.quote: has not provided sufficient credible evidence that he is personally at risk if he returns to Haiti

propositions.text: Objective evidence shows increasing crime in Haiti including gangs.
propositions.quote: objective evidence indicating that crime, including by various gangs, throughout Haiti is increasing

propositions.text: RPD restated finding no personal risk established for Principal Appellant if returned to Haiti.
propositions.quote: restated its finding that the Principal Appellant did not establish that he faces a personal risk if he returns to Haiti

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker found credibility undermined by failure to claim asylum and re-availment; insufficient personal risk evidence; crime increasing; restated no personal risk.

propositions.text: Appellants submit RPD erred by making decision perversely, ignoring corroborating evidence, and failing forward-looking risk assessment.
propositions.quote: RPD erred in: making its decision in a perverse or capricious manner without regard to the evidence presented; failing to analyze evidence which corroborated the personal risk

propositions.text: Appellants make multiple arguments supporting these submissions.
propositions.quote: The Appellants make a number of arguments to support their submissions.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD erred perversely, ignored corroborating evidence, and failed forward-looking risk assessment, supporting with multiple arguments.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD's positive determination for spouse corroborates Principal Appellant's allegations.
propositions.quote: RPD's positive determination of the refugee claim of the Principal Appellant's spouse was highly probative and corroborated his allegations

propositions.text: I disagree; spouse's positive determination based on her social group and gender-based persecution risk.
propositions.quote: I do not agree, The RPD made its positive determination based on the Principal Appellant's spouse's membership in a particular social group

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues spouse's positive determination corroborates Principal Appellant; court disagrees, noting basis was spouse's social group and gender risk.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred by searching for inconsistencies to discredit Principal Appellant.
propositions.quote: RPD erred as it simply searched through the Principal Appellant's testimony, looking for inconsistencies

propositions.text: I disagree; RPD based credibility finding on failure to claim protection and re-availment to Haiti.
propositions.quote: The RPD based its credibility finding on the Principal Appellant's failure to claim refugee protection after the XXXX XXXX, 2018, attack and his re-availment to Haiti

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD erred by seeking inconsistencies; court disagrees, finding credibility based on failure to claim protection and re-availment.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD unreasonably rejected Principal Appellant's return explanation corroborated by spouse and employer.
propositions.quote: RPD unreasonably rejected the Principal Appellant's explanation for his return to Haiti which was corroborated by his spouse and employer

propositions.text: Principal Appellant testified employer transferred him, he was threatened, resigned, fled Haiti, and claimed protection in Canada.
propositions.quote: he was traced and had threats from bandits... fearing risk to his life he resigned and fled Haiti on XXXX XXXX, 2018, and claimed protection of Canada

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues RPD unreasonably rejected Principal Appellant's return explanation corroborated by spouse and employer, involving threats and fleeing Haiti.

propositions.text: I agree RPD did not reference Principal Appellant's return explanation, so I will consider that evidence.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Appellants that the RPD did not reference the explanation for the Principal Appellant's return to Haiti, so I will consider that evidence

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees RPD did not reference return explanation and will consider that evidence.

propositions.text: Transcript shows no testimony from Principal Appellant or spouse on return reason; counsel made detailed submissions.
propositions.quote: neither the Principal Appellant nor his spouse gave any testimony about why the Principal Appellant returned to Haiti; however, their counsel did make detailed submissions

propositions.text: Principal Appellant's BOC says he returned home to work but continued to be attacked.
propositions.quote: I went back home, I think I could work in a different place but it was not a success. I continued to receive attack from different people

propositions.text: Spouse's statement closely matches Appellants' argument about threats and fleeing.
propositions.quote: His spouse's statement makes the Appellants' argument referenced above almost verbatim

paragraphs.summary: Court notes no testimony on return reason; counsel submitted; Principal Appellant's BOC and spouse's statement describe return and attacks.

propositions.text: Employer letters are inconsistent and contradictory about transfer, threats, and location.
propositions.quote: One letter... references a transfer... but no dates and no threats; another letter makes no reference to transfer; ID card says based in Port-au-Prince

propositions.text: Immigration form says Principal Appellant worked in Port-au-Prince from 2017 to 2018.
propositions.quote: immigration form... says that he worked in Port-au-Prince from XXXX 2017 to XXXX 2018

paragraphs.summary: Court finds employer letters inconsistent and immigration form shows work in Port-au-Prince 2017-2018.

propositions.text: Evidence corroborating Principal Appellant's return explanation is inconsistent and harms credibility.
propositions.quote: evidence which would corroborate the Principal Appellant's explanation for returning to Haiti in July 2018 is inconsistent and contradictory, which adversely impacts the credibility

paragraphs.summary: Court finds corroborating evidence for return explanation inconsistent and harms credibility.

propositions.text: Appellants submit RPD erred by failing to assess crucial documentary evidence in section 97 prospective risk analysis.
propositions.quote: RPD erred as it failed to acknowledge and assess crucial documentary evidence in its section 97 analysis

propositions.text: I agree RPD did not do full prospective risk analysis or reference Appellants' documentary evidence, so I have done so.
propositions.quote: I agree that the RPD did not undertake a fulsome prospective risk analysis or reference the Appellants documentary evidence, so I have done so

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits RPD failed to assess documentary evidence in prospective risk; court agrees and has done so.

propositions.text: Determining protection need involves analyzing risk nature, likelihood, and whether risk is general or personal.
propositions.quote: A determination of whether the Principal Appellant is a person in need of protection involves an analysis of the nature of the risk at issue, of the likelihood that the Principal Appellant would be subject to that risk, and, if so, whether the same risk is faced generally by others

paragraphs.summary: Court states protection determination requires analyzing risk nature, likelihood, and whether risk is personal or general.

propositions.text: Federal Court summarized two-part test for section 97: identify ongoing risk, then compare risk to significant group to assess protection entitlement.
propositions.quote: First, the RPD should consider whether there is an ongoing future risk... compare the risk faced by the claimant to that faced by a significant group... claimant will be entitled to protection under section 97

propositions.text: Second step is forward-looking, comparing claimant's future risk to general population risk, not cause of risk.
propositions.quote: the second step in the inquiry "is a forward-looking inquiry and is concerned not so much with the cause of the risk but rather with the likelihood of what will happen to the claimant in the future

paragraphs.summary: Prior court explains section 97 test: identify ongoing risk, then compare claimant's risk to significant group forward-looking.

propositions.text: First step: characterize nature of risk, determine if ongoing future risk and if cruel or unusual treatment.
propositions.quote: First, the RPD must correctly characterize the nature of the risk faced by the claimant... whether the risk is one of cruel or unusual treatment or punishment

paragraphs.summary: Prior court states first step is to characterize nature of risk and determine if ongoing and cruel or unusual.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant not personally targeted in 2018 incidents; attackers unidentified.
propositions.quote: I find that the Principal Appellant has not established that he was personally targeted in the XXXX and XXXX 2018 incidents

propositions.text: No evidence links father-in-law's 2018-2019 incidents to Principal Appellant; fire started on neighbouring property.
propositions.quote: no evidence presented to suggest that the two incidents faced by the Principal Appellant's father-in-law in 2018 and 2019 had anything to do with the Principal Appellant

propositions.text: Principal Appellant's testimony about threats embellishes police report; no evidence attackers same in all incidents.
propositions.quote: This testimony, however, embellishes the police report filed by his mother... There is nothing in the evidence which demonstrated that it was the same "unidentified" criminals

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Principal Appellant not personally targeted; no link to father-in-law's incidents; testimony embellishes police report; attackers unidentified.

propositions.text: Risk faced is random criminal acts by unidentified perpetrators perceiving wealth; ongoing future risk in Haiti.
propositions.quote: the nature of the risk faced by the Principal Appellant is that of random criminal acts by unidentified perpetrators who possibly perceive him to be wealthy and it is an ongoing future risk in Haiti

paragraphs.summary: Court finds risk is random crime by unidentified perpetrators perceiving wealth; ongoing future risk in Haiti.

propositions.text: Next step is comparing Principal Appellant's risk to that faced by significant group in Haiti to assess similarity.
propositions.quote: The next step is to compare the risk faced by the Principal Appellant to that faced by a significant group in Haiti

paragraphs.summary: Court states next step is comparing Principal Appellant's risk to significant group in Haiti.

propositions.text: Appellants submit they face serious threats, robbery, kidnapping, and death as wealthy returnees if returned to Haiti.
propositions.quote: if they return to Haiti they will face serious threats, robbed, kidnapped and killed as they are considered wealthy

paragraphs.summary: Applicant submits they face serious threats and harm as wealthy returnees if returned to Haiti.

propositions.text: Objective evidence shows pervasive criminality in Haiti affecting rich and poor indiscriminately.
propositions.quote: criminality is pervasive in Haiti and affects a large segment of the population and appears to be indiscriminate, affecting rich and poor alike

propositions.text: New evidence confirms upsurge in violence by armed gangs especially in slums and impoverished areas.
propositions.quote: new evidence presented by the Appellants confirms "an upsurge in violence caused by armed gangs" especially in the slums and impoverished neighbourhoods of Haiti

paragraphs.summary: Court notes objective evidence of pervasive criminality affecting all and new evidence of gang violence upsurge in poor areas.

propositions.text: The Appellants' new evidence says Haitians returning after a long stay abroad risk being targeted by criminals as they are considered wealthy.
propositions.quote: The Appellants' new evidence, document D,55 an Immigration and Refugee Board Response to Information Request (2020 RIR)56 is mixed. It says that Haitians returning to Haiti after a long stay abroad risk being targeted by criminals because they are considered to be wealthy

propositions.text: Young returnees are more frequent targets of criminals than senior citizens who are treated with respect and compassion.
propositions.quote: and that young returnees are more frequent targets of criminals than senior citizens who are treated with a measure of respect and compassion

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues new evidence says Haitian returnees risk criminal targeting, especially young returnees, unlike senior citizens treated with respect.

propositions.text: The 2020 RIR says risks depend on fleeing political violence, witnessing crime, being accused, unpaid loans, communal violence, and faction allegiance.
propositions.quote: The 2020 RIR says that risks a returnee will face depend on the following factors: whether or not the individual fled the community because of political violence; was the witness of a crime; has been accused of a crime; incurred loans that they will not be able to repay; and was caught up in communal violence and has allegiance to a faction

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the 2020 RIR identifies risk factors for returnees including political violence, crime witness, accusations, debts, communal violence, and faction allegiance.

propositions.text: The 2020 RIR says kidnapping risk is indiscriminate and widespread, affecting all Haitians regardless of rank or social class.
propositions.quote: The 2020 RIR also says the risk of kidnapping for ransom, for example, is indiscriminate and widespread; members of the general Haitian population, regardless of their rank or social class, are at risk of being kidnapped and everyone is at risk

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the 2020 RIR states kidnapping risk is widespread and indiscriminate among all Haitians regardless of social status.

propositions.text: All Haitians, rich and poor, are at risk from bandits and gangs.
propositions.quote: The evidence is that all Haitians, rich and poor, are at risk of being targeted by bandits and gangs

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant is nearly 40, has not lived long in Canada, and is not in high-risk categories identified in 2020 RIR.
propositions.quote: The Principal Appellant has not lived in Canada for a long time, is approaching 40 years old and is not in the high-risk categories identified in the 2020 RIR

propositions.text: The Principal Appellant has not shown on balance of probabilities that his risk differs from most Haitians' risk.
propositions.quote: I find that the Principal Appellant has not established, on a balance of probabilities, that his personal situation would subject him to a risk any different from that faced by most of the Haitian population

paragraphs.summary: The court finds all Haitians face risk; the Principal Appellant is not high-risk and has not proven a different personal risk.

propositions.text: The appeal is dismissed and the RPD decision confirmed that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellants are not refugees or in need of protection.
